text.p: French far-rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen has called on young members of his National Front to prepare themselves for revolution, predicting that the country's political system would collapse.
"It is certain only the National Front can rescue the country from decadence," Le Pen told leaders of the Front's youth wing gathered at a weekend party congress.

"At some point, all this will stop and then the revolution will occur...At some point the worm-eaten structures of our system will collapse," he said. "Prepare your hearts and minds...because at some point the people will call us."
Le Pen, already embroiled in controversy over his open espousal of racial inequality, gave no details of the approaching "revolution", but said the far-left was already preparing for it.
A spokesman for the Front confirmed excerpts of the speech which were published on Monday by the daily Le Monde.
Numerous political leaders called on the government to prosecute Le Pen for inciting racial hatred, or to ban his party, after he said racial inequality was obvious.
Local by-elections nonetheless pointed to a continuing rise in popularity for Le Pen and his anti-immigrant Front, which won 15 percent of the vote in last year's presidential elections.
The Front improved its results in the first round of three of four by-elections held on Sunday although none of its candidates attained the 50 percent required to avoid a run-off.

In Toulon, one of the first three muncipalities won by the movement last year, Front candidate Gerard Bauer finished on top with 34.4 percent of the votes compared with 18.3 percent in the last such election two years ago.
An opinion poll published on Monday exposed confusion in voters' attitudes to the Front, saying that while most voters viewed it as racist, a narrow majority backed some of its views.
The Ipsos survey, conducted after Le Pen's remarks on racial inequality, found that 71 percent believe the National Front to be a racist party but 51 percent approved some of its ideas.

Justice Minister Jacques Toubon has announced he will try to tighten anti-racism laws after Le Pen said last week that racial inequality was "a fact", a statement vague enough to avoid punishment under existing laws against inciting racial hatred.
The Ipsos poll, of 956 voters interviewed on Friday and Saturday, said 63 percent of voters were shocked by Le Pen's statement, and 71 percent favoured stiffening the laws.

Mainstream politicians have savaged Le Pen for espousing racial inequality, but almost all have shied away from a Socialist proposal to ban the Front, fearing this would cause a backlash of sympathy for his anti-immigrant views.

Hardline former interior minister Charles Pasqua came out strongly against Le Pen in a political rally on Sunday night, saying the weight of the law should fall on those "who shamelessly spread theories alien to the dignity of man".
Pasqua was the architect of tough 1993 laws to curb immigration which were at the time described by critics as pandering to the National Front.
